arXiv:2511.12665v3 [math.OC] 30 Jul 2026

The iterates of FISTA converge even under
inexact computations and stochastic gradients

Saverio Salzo ††thanks: Sapienza Università di Roma, Via Ariosto 25, 00185, Roma, Italy (saverio.salzo@uniroma1.it)††thanks: Istituto Italiano di Tecnologia, Via E.˜Melen 83, 16152, Genova, Italy
Abstract

Very recently, the papers “Point Convergence of Nesterov’s Accelerated Gradient Method: An AI-Assisted Proof” by Jang and Ryu, and “The Iterates of Nesterov’s Accelerated Algorithm Converge in the Critical Regimes” by Boţ, Fadili, and Nguyen have simultaneously resolved a long-standing open problem concerning Nesterov’s accelerated gradient method. These works show that the iterates of the algorithm (known in its composite form as FISTA) indeed converge to an optimal solution. In this work, we extend these results and prove that, in infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces, the iterates of such an algorithm still converge (in the weak sense) even when the proximity operator and the gradient are computed inexactly, with the latter possibly stochastic.

Keywords. Convex optimization, accelerated proximal gradient algorithms, inexact algorithms, stochastic optimization, convergence of the iterates, convergence rates.
AMS Mathematics Subject Classification: 65K05, 90C25, 90C15, 49M27

1 Introduction

In this paper, we address the composite convex optimization problem

minx∈ℋ⁡f⁡(x)+g⁡(x)=:F⁡(x),\min_{x\in\mathcal{H}}f(x)+g(x)=:F(x), (1.1)

under the following assumption.

Assumption 1.

ℋ\mathcal{H} is a real Hilbert space, the function f:ℋ→ℝf\colon\mathcal{H}\to\mathbb{R} is convex and differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradient, with constant L>0L>0, the function g:ℋ→]−∞,+∞]g\colon\mathcal{H}\to\left]-\infty,+\infty\right] is extended real-valued, proper, convex and lower semicontinuous, and the set of minimizers of F:=f+gF:=f+g is nonempty.

This framework covers a wide range of problems in signal processing, machine learning, and inverse problems, and is classically addressed by first-order proximal algorithms.

Among them, the Fast Iterative Shrinkage-Thresholding Algorithm (FISTA), introduced by Beck and Teboulle in [10] and rooted in Nesterov’s seminal acceleration technique [21] and its extension to the proximal point algorithm given by Güler in [18], stands out for achieving the optimal O⁡(1/k2)O(1/k^{2}) convergence rate in objective values in the convex setting. FISTA and its continuous-time analogues have been the subject of intense study in recent years (see, e.g., [2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 14, 28] and references therein), due to both their practical efficiency and the long-standing theoretical question concerning the convergence of the iterates themselves.

Originally, Nesterov [21] established convergence rates for the objective values, but not for the iterates. The first substantial progress in this direction was achieved by Chambolle and Dossal [14], who proved the convergence of the iterates in the noncritical regime—that is, under specific constraints on the acceleration parameters. Subsequent works such as [6, 5, 12] further investigate rates of convergence and connections with other acceleration schemes such as the Heavy Ball method by Polyak [23].

On the other hand, several studies have focused on the analysis of inexact versions of the method [7, 8, 11, 27, 29], where both the gradient and the proximity operator may be computed only approximately, allowing for numerical truncation and/or inner iterative schemes. This line of research was initiated in [29, 27], where convergence rates in objective values were derived. Subsequently, the work [7] extended this analysis to the convergence of the iterates, but only in the noncritical regime. As a result, understanding the behaviour of the iterates in the original Nesterov’s accelerated method (the critical regime) has eluded researchers for more than a decade.

Very recently, two independent works, by Jang and Ryu [19], and by Boţ, Fadili, and Nguyen [13], have simultaneously resolved this long-standing open problem. They proved that the iterates of Nesterov’s accelerated algorithm converge even in the critical regime—[19] covers the smooth finite dimensional case, while [13] addresses the nonsmooth case, thus FISTA, in infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces. The proof is surprisingly simple and was originally triggered by Ryu [25] who announced on X that he had proved the convergence of the trajectory of the corresponding continuous-time accelerated dynamics, relying heavily on ChatGPT.

1.1 Our contribution

Building upon the recent advances mentioned above, we establish the weak convergence of the iterates of an inexact version of FISTA in infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. In addition, we prove the almost-sure weak convergence of the iterates when the inexact gradient is stochastic, thereby extending the deterministic theory to a stochastic setting. The deterministic algorithm allows for errors both in the computation of the gradient and in the evaluation of the proximity operator, modeled through the inexactness criterion given in [26, 27]. In contrast, the stochastic algorithm, beyond the above cited type of errors in the proximity operator, also permits gradient evaluations corrupted by random noise, provided the noise has uniformly bounded variance. The analysis covers the critical regime, matching the strength of the exact results in [19, 13], while encompassing earlier partial results such as those in [7]. In particular, compared to this latter work, our proof takes advantage of the ideas in [19] and ultimately is both simpler and more general, removing also the spurious assumption of coercivity of FF. The argument relies on: (1) the analysis of a recursive numerical inequality that (via a discrete version of the Bihari-La Salle Lemma) allows to control the errors while ensuring convergence of the Lyapunov function (even though it is no longer decreasing), (2) an adaptation of Opial’s Lemma suitable for accelerated schemes, which is also extended to random sequences, and (3) following [19], a Lemma originally given in [12], that yields a representation of the iterates as convex combinations. Finally, similarly to [7], we highlight the balance between the required decay of the error terms and the chosen acceleration parameter, thereby bridging the gap between the classical proximal gradient method and its fully accelerated counterpart.

1.2 Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 1.3, we set the notation and present the two algorithms that are the focus of this study. Section 2 collects the basic facts needed for the convergence analysis. In Section 3, after presenting several properties of the acceleration parameters of FISTA and providing some additional preparatory lemmas, we state the two main theorems of the paper. Finally, for reader’s convenience and for completeness we provide in Appendix A some proofs of the facts presented in Section 2.

1.3 Notation and definition of the algorithms

We denote by ℋ⊕ℋ\mathcal{H}\oplus\mathcal{H} the direct sum of ℋ\mathcal{H} with itself, meaning the vector space ℋ×ℋ\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} endowed with the scalar product ((x1,x2),(y1,y2))↦⟨x1,y1⟩+⟨x2,y2⟩((x_{1},x_{2}),(y_{1},y_{2}))\mapsto\langle{x_{1},y_{1}}\rangle+\langle{x_{2},y_{2}}\rangle. When ε=0\varepsilon=0, we simply write ∂φ\partial\varphi, which is called the subdifferential of φ\varphi. The proximity operator of φ\varphi is defined as

proxφ:ℋ→ℋ:x↦argmin{φ+12‖⋅−x‖2},\prox_{\varphi}\colon\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{H}\colon x\mapsto\argmin\Big\{\varphi+\frac{1}{2}\left\|{\,\cdot\,-x}\right\|^{2}\Big\},

Moreover, the proximity operator is nonexpansive, meaning that ‖proxφ⁡(x)−proxφ⁡(y)‖≤‖x−y‖\left\|{\prox_{\varphi}(x)-\prox_{\varphi}(y)}\right\|\leq\left\|{x-y}\right\|, for every x,y∈ℋx,y\in\mathcal{H} (see [9]). A numerical sequence (αk)k∈ℕ(\alpha_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is increasing (resp. decreasing) if αk≤αk+1\alpha_{k}\leq\alpha_{k+1} (resp. αk≥αk+1\alpha_{k}\geq\alpha_{k+1}), for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. A sequential weak cluster point of a sequence (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is the limit of any weakly converging subsequence. We recall that in a Hilbert space any bounded sequence always admits a weakly converging subsequence, so it has at least a sequential weak cluster point [9]. We conclude this paragraph, by setting the notation for random variables and their (conditional) expectations. The underlying probability space will be denoted by (Ω,𝔄,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P}). If ℋ\mathcal{H} is separable, vv is a ℋ\mathcal{H}-valued random variable which is integrable, and 𝔉⊂𝔄\mathfrak{F}\subset\mathfrak{A} is a sub-σ\sigma-algebra of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, the (conditional) expectation of vv (given 𝔉\mathfrak{F}) is denoted by 𝔼⁡[v]\mathbb{E}[v] (resp. 𝔼⁡[v|𝔉]\mathbb{E}[v\,|\,\mathfrak{F}]). We recall that if ww is another random vector which is measurable w.r.t. 𝔉\mathfrak{F}, then 𝔼⁡[⟨v,w⟩|𝔉]=⟨𝔼⁡[v|𝔉],w⟩\mathbb{E}[\langle{v,w}\rangle\,|\,\mathfrak{F}]=\langle{\mathbb{E}[v\,|\,\mathfrak{F}],w}\rangle. The conditional expectation can be also defined for positive real-valued random variable, without any integrability condition.

In what follows, we present two versions of FISTA, one with deterministic errors and one with stochastic errors. Both rely on the following notion of an inexact proximity operator, introduced and analyzed in detail in [26] and subsequently used, among others, in [27, 29, 7].

2 The basic facts

In this section, we present some fundamental facts upon which the main proof is built. Some of them are well-known in the related literature, while others are more recent and possibly less familiar.

Fact 2.1.

Let (αk)k∈ℕ(\alpha_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (εk)k∈ℕ(\varepsilon_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} such that ∑k∈ℕεk<+∞\sum_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\varepsilon_{k}<+\infty and

(∀k∈ℕ)αk+1−αk≤εk.(\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N})\quad\alpha_{k+1}-\alpha_{k}\leq\varepsilon_{k}. (2.1)

Then (αk)k∈ℕ(\alpha_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent.

Remark 2.2.

In the above result, the sequence (αk)k∈ℕ(\alpha_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} can be seen as decreasing up to summable errors. Thus, Fact 2.1 establishes that such sequences are convergent.

The next fact is a discrete version of a special case of the classical Bihari–LaSalle Lemma. To the best of our knowledge it first appeared in the literature related to convex optimization in [27], in the study of rates of convergence for the inexact FISTA—although it was not explicitly linked to the Bihari–LaSalle Lemma. In Appendix A we provide a proof that is more direct of the one in [27] and follows the same ideas of the continuous version.

Fact 2.3 (Bihari–LaSalle Lemma, discrete version).

Let (μk)k∈ℕ(\mu_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (λk)k∈ℕ(\lambda_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be two sequences in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} and (σk)k∈ℕ(\sigma_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be an increasing sequence in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} such that

∀k∈ℕ:μk≤σk+∑i=0kλi​μi.\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N}\colon\mu_{k}\leq\sigma_{k}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\sqrt{\mu_{i}}.

Then, for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, max0≤i≤k⁡μi≤12​∑i=0kλi+((12​∑i=0kλi)2+σk)1/2≤∑i=0kλi+σk\displaystyle\max_{0\leq i\leq k}\sqrt{\mu_{i}}\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}+\bigg(\Big(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\Big)^{2}+\sigma_{k}\bigg)^{1/2}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}+\sqrt{\sigma_{k}}.

The following result is known as Opial’s Lemma (see e.g., [9, Lemma 2.47]). We include its proof here, since in the subsequent remark we slightly weaken the assumptions to make it more useful for our purposes. Later, in Lemma 3.5 we will give also a stochastic version. This is one of the points in which the analysis of convergence of the iterates of Nesterov’s accelerated method diverges from the classical analysis of fixed-point iterations of a nonexpansive operator—which includes that of the (nonaccelerated) proximal gradient algorithm.

Fact 2.4 (Opial Lemma).

Let S⊂ℋS\subset\mathcal{H} be nonempty. Let (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence in ℋ\mathcal{H} and suppose that the sequential weak cluster points of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} belong to SS and that for any y∈Sy\in S, (‖xk−y‖)k∈ℕ(\left\|{x_{k}-y}\right\|)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent. Then (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} weakly converges to a point in SS.

Proof.

The assumptions ensure that (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded. Therefore, the set of sequential weak cluster points of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is nonempty. Let y1,y2∈ℋy_{1},y_{2}\in\mathcal{H} be two sequential weak cluster points of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, so that there exist two subsequences (xk1)k∈ℕ(x_{k}^{1})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (xk2)k∈ℕ(x_{k}^{2})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, such that xk1⇀y1x_{k}^{1}\rightharpoonup y_{1} and xk2⇀y2x_{k}^{2}\rightharpoonup y_{2}. Then, for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},

‖xk−y1‖2−‖xk−y2‖2=2​⟨xk,y2−y1⟩+‖y1‖2−‖y2‖2.\left\|{x_{k}-y_{1}}\right\|^{2}-\left\|{x_{k}-y_{2}}\right\|^{2}=2\langle{x_{k},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle+\left\|{y_{1}}\right\|^{2}-\left\|{y_{2}}\right\|^{2}. (2.2)

Since y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} are sequential weak cluster points of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, by assumptions, y1,y2∈Sy_{1},y_{2}\in S and (‖xk−y1‖)k∈ℕ(\left\|{x_{k}-y_{1}}\right\|)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (‖xk−y2‖)k∈ℕ(\left\|{x_{k}-y_{2}}\right\|)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} are convergent. Therefore by (2.2), we obtain that there exists β∈ℝ\beta\in\mathbb{R} such that ⟨xk,y2−y1⟩→β\langle{x_{k},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle\to\beta. Now, since xki⇀yix_{k}^{i}\rightharpoonup y_{i}, i=1,2i=1,2, we have ⟨xki,y2−y1⟩→⟨yi,y2−y1⟩\langle{x_{k}^{i},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle\to\langle{y_{i},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle, which implies

⟨y1,y2−y1⟩=β=⟨y2,y2−y1⟩\langle{y_{1},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle=\beta=\langle{y_{2},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle

and hence ‖y2−y1‖2=0\left\|{y_{2}-y_{1}}\right\|^{2}=0. This proves that the set of sequential weak cluster points of the sequence (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a singleton contained in SS. So, the sequence (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is weakly convergent to a point in SS. ∎

Remark 2.5.

It is clear from the proof above that Opial’s Lemma remains true if the condition that (‖xk−y‖2)k∈ℕ(\left\|{x_{k}-y}\right\|^{2})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent for any y∈Sy\in S, is replaced by the following two:

  • •

    (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded

  • •

    ∀y1,y2∈S:(⟨xk,y2−y1⟩)k∈ℕ\forall\,y_{1},y_{2}\in S\colon(\langle{x_{k},y_{2}-y_{1}}\rangle)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent.

The next result is the second pivotal ingredient to handle the convergence of the iterates of Nesterov’s accelerated method.

Fact 2.6 ([12], Lemma A.4).

Let (ak)k∈ℕ(a_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be sequence of real numbers and let (λk)k∈ℕ(\lambda_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence in ℝ+⁣+\mathbb{R}_{++}. Let ℓ∈ℝ\ell\in\mathbb{R} and suppose that ∑k=0+∞1/λk=+∞\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}1/\lambda_{k}=+\infty. Then

ak+1+λk​(ak+1−ak)→ℓ⇒ak→ℓ.a_{k+1}+\lambda_{k}(a_{k+1}-a_{k})\to\ell\ \Rightarrow\ a_{k}\to\ell.
Proof (Sketch).

Set bk=ak+1+λk​(ak+1−ak)b_{k}=a_{k+1}+\lambda_{k}(a_{k+1}-a_{k}). The crux of the proof is to show that each aka_{k} can be seen as weighted sum of the terms a0,b0,…,bk−1a_{0},b_{0},\dots,b_{k-1} for certain weights wiw_{i}’s such that ∑i=0kwi→+∞\sum_{i=0}^{k}w_{i}\to+\infty as k→+∞k\to+\infty. Then the conclusion follows from the Cesàro mean theorem. Full details are given in Appendix A. ∎

We conclude by presenting the classical Robbins–Siegmund Theorem on almost supermartingales, that will be at the basis of the analysis of the stochastic version of FISTA.

Fact 2.7 (Robbins–Siegmund Theorem [24]).

Let (𝔉k)k∈ℕ(\mathfrak{F}_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be a filtration on (Ω,𝔄,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P}) and let (ξk)k∈ℕ(\xi_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, (χk)k∈ℕ(\chi_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, (εk)k∈ℕ(\varepsilon_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, and (ζk)k∈ℕ(\zeta_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences of positive real-valued random variables which are adapted to (𝔉k)k∈ℕ(\mathfrak{F}_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}. Suppose that

  1. (i)

    ∑k=0+∞χk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}\chi_{k}<+\infty and ∑k=0+∞εk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}\varepsilon_{k}<+\infty a.s.

  2. (ii)

    for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, 𝔼⁡[ξk+1|𝔉k]≤(1+χk)​ξk+εk−ζk\mathbb{E}[\xi_{k+1}\,|\,\mathfrak{F}_{k}]\leq(1+\chi_{k})\xi_{k}+\varepsilon_{k}-\zeta_{k}.

Then there exists a positive real-valued random variable ξ\xi such that ξk→ξ\xi_{k}\to\xi a.s. and ∑k=0+∞ζk<+∞\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}\zeta_{k}<+\infty a.s.

3 Analysis of the convergence

Throughout the rest of the paper we make Assumption 1 and we set

F∗=minx∈ℋ⁡F⁡(x)andS∗=argminx∈ℋF​(x).F_{*}=\min_{x\in\mathcal{H}}F(x)\quad\text{and}\quad S_{*}=\argmin_{x\in\mathcal{H}}F(x).

3.1 The acceleration parameters

We start by clarifying the condition

t0=1and∀k∈ℕ,k≥1: 1≤tkandtk2−tk−tk−12≤0,t_{0}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N},\,k\geq 1\colon\ \ 1\leq t_{k}\ \ \text{and}\ \ t_{k}^{2}-t_{k}-t_{k-1}^{2}\leq 0, (3.1)

on the parameters tkt_{k}’s in Algorithms 1.3 and 1.4. A numerical sequence (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} satisfying (3.1) will be called a sequence of admissible parameters for FISTA.

We note that, by solving the above quadratic inequality in tkt_{k}, condition (3.1) can be equivalently written as

t0=1and∀k∈ℕ,k≥1: 1≤tk≤1+1+4​tk−122=:φ⁡(tk−1),t_{0}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N},\,k\geq 1\colon\ \ 1\leq t_{k}\leq\frac{1+\sqrt{1+4t_{k-1}^{2}}}{2}=:\varphi(t_{k-1}), (3.2)

where φ:[1,+∞[→[1,+∞[:t↦(1+1+4​t2)/2\varphi\colon\left[1,+\infty\right[\to\left[1,+\infty\right[\colon t\mapsto\big(1+\sqrt{1+4t^{2}}\big)/2. It is easy to see that the function φ\varphi satisfies the following properties

  1. (i)

    ∀t≥1\forall\,t\geq 1, φ⁡(t)−t>1/2\varphi(t)-t>1/2

  2. (ii)

    φ⁡(t)−t↓1/2\varphi(t)-t\downarrow 1/2 as t↑+∞t\uparrow+\infty.

Below we collect the main properties of sequences of admissible parameters for FISTA.

Proposition 3.1.

Let (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+}. The following hold.

  2. (ii)

    (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is an increasing sequence of admissible parameters for FISTA iff

    t0=1and∀k∈ℕ,k≥1:tk∈[tk−1,φ⁡(tk−1)].t_{0}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N},\,k\geq 1\colon t_{k}\in[t_{k-1},\varphi(t_{k-1})]. (3.3)

    Given a∈[2,+∞[a\in\left[2,+\infty\right[, suppose that (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} satisfies the stronger condition22 2 Recall that the length of the interval [tk−1,φ⁡(tk−1)][t_{k-1},\varphi(t_{k-1})] is strictly greater then 1/21/2.

    t0=1and∀k∈ℕ:k≥1:tk∈[tk−1+1/a,φ⁡(tk−1)].t_{0}=1\quad\text{and}\quad\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N}\colon k\geq 1\colon t_{k}\in[t_{k-1}+1/a,\varphi(t_{k-1})]. (3.4)

    Then, ∀k∈ℕ,k≥1\forall\,k\in\mathbb{N},\,k\geq 1, tk−tk−1≥1/at_{k}-t_{k-1}\geq 1/a and hence k+aa≤tk≤k+1\frac{k+a}{a}\leq t_{k}\leq k+1, so that tk≍kt_{k}\asymp k.

  4. (iv)

    Given α∈]0,1[\alpha\in\left]0,1\right[, if (sk)k∈ℕ(s_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence of admissible parameters for FISTA, then (tk)k∈ℕ≡(skα)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\equiv(s_{k}^{\alpha})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is a sequence of admissible parameters for FISTA too.

3.2 Three preparatory lemmas

We now present a perturbed version of the basic inequality of the proximal gradient descent algorithm. This result was essentially given in [27] (see also [7]).

and hence

Next, we prove a general bound concerning a recursive inequality that is encoutered in the convergence analysis of Algorithm 1.3 and Algorithm 1.4. This result will allow to control the errors along the iterations while keeping the underlying Lyapunov function converging, although it does not decrease anymore.

Lemma 3.4.

Let (αk)k∈ℕ,(λk)k∈ℕ(\alpha_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}},(\lambda_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (ξk)k∈ℕ(\xi_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be sequences in ℝ+\mathbb{R}_{+} such that

∀k∈ℕ:αk+1≤αk+λk​αk+1+ξk.\displaystyle\forall k\in\mathbb{N}\colon\alpha_{k+1}\leq\alpha_{k}+\lambda_{k}\sqrt{\alpha_{k+1}}+\xi_{k}. (3.7)

Then the following hold for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}

    max0≤i≤k+1⁡αi≤∑i=0kλi+α0+∑i=0kξi\displaystyle\max_{0\leq i\leq k+1}\sqrt{\alpha_{i}}\leq\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}+\sqrt{\alpha_{0}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\xi_{i}}.

    αk+1≤109​(α0+∑i=0kξi)+(∑i=0kλi)2\displaystyle\alpha_{k+1}\leq\frac{10}{9}\bigg(\alpha_{0}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\xi_{i}\bigg)+\bigg(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\bigg)^{\!2}.

Proof.

(i): By summing the inequality αi+1−αi≤λi​αi+1+ξi\alpha_{i+1}-\alpha_{i}\leq\lambda_{i}\sqrt{\alpha_{i+1}}+\xi_{i} from i=0i=0 to i=ki=k, we obtain

αk+1≤α0+∑i=0kξi+∑i=0kλi​αi+1.\alpha_{k+1}\leq\alpha_{0}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\xi_{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\sqrt{\alpha_{i+1}}. (3.8)

Thus, setting σk=α0+∑i=0kξi\sigma_{k}=\alpha_{0}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\xi_{i}, we have

∀k∈ℕ:αk+1≤σk+∑i=0kλi​αi+1.\forall k\in\mathbb{N}\colon\ \alpha_{k+1}\leq\sigma_{k}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\sqrt{\alpha_{i+1}}.

(ii): Setting Ak=max0≤i≤k⁡αi+1A_{k}=\max_{0\leq i\leq k}\sqrt{\alpha_{i+1}}, we derive from (i), that, for every ε,δ>0\varepsilon,\delta>0

≤14​ε​δ​(∑i=0kλi)2+δ4​ε​(α0+∑i=0kξi)+ε2​(∑i=0kλi)2.\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{4\varepsilon\delta}\bigg(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\bigg)^{2}+\frac{\delta}{4\varepsilon}\bigg(\alpha_{0}+\sum_{i=0}^{k}\xi_{i}\bigg)+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\bigg(\sum_{i=0}^{k}\lambda_{i}\bigg)^{2}.

Concerning the final part of the statement we note that, thanks to (ii), if (λk)k∈ℕ(\lambda_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (ξk)k∈ℕ(\xi_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} are summable, then (αk+1)k∈ℕ(\sqrt{\alpha_{k+1}})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded, say by M≥0M\geq 0 and hence the recursive inequality (3.7) yields αk+1≤αk+(λk​M+ξk)\alpha_{k+1}\leq\alpha_{k}+(\lambda_{k}M+\xi_{k}) and the statement follows from Fact 2.1. ∎

We conclude the section by giving a stochastic version of the Opial’s Lemma that will be critical for the analysis of Algorithm 1.4. This is a generalization of [17, Proposition 2.3] in the spirit of Remark 2.5 above.

Lemma 3.5 (Stochastic Opial’s Lemma).

Let ℋ\mathcal{H} be a separable real Hilbert space, let S⊂ℋS\subset\mathcal{H} be nonempty and let (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be a sequence of random vectors on the probability space (Ω,𝔄,ℙ)\left(\Omega,\mathfrak{A},\mathbb{P}\right) with values in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Suppose that the following two conditions hold.

  1. (a)

    (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded a.s.

  2. (b)

    for every y1,y2∈Sy_{1},y_{2}\in S, there exists Ωy1,y2∈𝔄\Omega_{y_{1},y_{2}}\in\mathfrak{A}, with ℙ⁡(Ωy1,y2)=1\mathbb{P}(\Omega_{y_{1},y_{2}})=1, such that, for every ω∈Ωy1,y2\omega\in\Omega_{y_{1},y_{2}}, the sequence (⟨xk​(ω),y1−y2⟩)k∈ℕ(\langle{x_{k}(\omega),y_{1}-y_{2}}\rangle)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} converges.

Then, there exists Ω~∈𝔄\tilde{\Omega}\in\mathfrak{A}, with ℙ⁡(Ω~)=1\mathbb{P}(\tilde{\Omega})=1, such that, for every ω∈Ω~\omega\in\tilde{\Omega}, (xk​(ω))k∈ℕ(x_{k}(\omega))_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded and for every y1,y2,∈Sy_{1},y_{2},\in S, (⟨xk​(ω),y1−y2⟩)k∈ℕ(\langle{x_{k}(\omega),y_{1}-y_{2}}\rangle)_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is convergent. Moreover, if the following additional condition hold

  1. (c)

    the set of sequential weak cluster points of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is contained in SS almost surely,

then there exists an SS-valued random vector x¯\bar{x} such that xk⇀x¯x_{k}\rightharpoonup\bar{x} a.s.

Proof.

We prove the first part of the statement. Since SS is a subset of a separable metric space, it is separable. Let D⊂SD\subset S be countable and dense in SS and let Ω~1=⋂z1,z2∈DΩz1,z2\tilde{\Omega}_{1}=\bigcap_{z_{1},z_{2}\in D}\Omega_{z_{1},z_{2}}. (⟨xk​(ω),z1−z2⟩)k∈ℕ​is convergent.(\langle{x_{k}(\omega),z_{1}-z_{2}}\rangle)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\ \text{is convergent.}

3.3 The two main theorems

Finally, we are ready to provide the first main result of the paper.

Remark 3.7.
  1. (i)

    Depending on the asymptotic behavior of the sequence (tk)k∈ℕ(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}, the summability conditions on the errors may be more or less demanding: in particular, if tkt_{k} is defined by any of the two choices in (3.6) with α∈]0,1]\alpha\in\left]0,1\right] (recall Proposition 3.1(iii)-(iv)), then they become

    ∑k=0+∞kα​δk<+∞and∑k=0+∞kα​‖bk‖<+∞,\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}k^{\alpha}\delta_{k}<+\infty\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}k^{\alpha}\left\|{b_{k}}\right\|<+\infty, (3.16)

    which are ensured if both δk\delta_{k} and ‖bk‖\left\|{b_{k}}\right\| are O⁡(1/kp)O(1/k^{p}) with p>1+αp>1+\alpha; and in such case 1−βk≍1/kα1-\beta_{k}\asymp 1/k^{\alpha} and F⁡(xk)−F∗=O⁡(1/k2​α)F(x_{k})-F_{*}=O(1/k^{2\alpha}). We stress that in all the spectrum of values α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] the iterates of Algorithm 1.3 are ensured to weakly converge to a solution of problem (1.1). Moreover, concerning the speed of convergence in objective values the same remarks given in [7] fully apply here too. Thus, we have full acceleration when α=1\alpha=1, but this corresponds to the strongest assumptions on the error decay. Conversely, if we slowdown the acceleration by choosing α∈]0,1[\alpha\in\left]0,1\right[, the requirements on the error decay become less stringent. Finally, we note that if α=0\alpha=0, (tk)k∈ℕ≡1(t_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\equiv 1, Algorithm 1.3 turns to the (nonaccelerated) proximal gradient algorithm and the conditions (3.16) just state the summability of the error sequences (δk)k∈ℕ(\delta_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (‖bk‖)k∈ℕ(\left\|{b_{k}}\right\|)_{k\in\mathbb{N}}. This is in full agreement with well-known facts about the inexact proximal gradient algorithm (see e.g. [16]).

  2. (ii)

    The condition tk→+∞t_{k}\to+\infty is ensured if the tkt_{k}’s satisfy (3.4) and in particular if they are defined according to any of the two choices in (3.5).

Remark 3.8.

Theorem 3.6 guarantees that if tkt_{k} is defined by any of the two choices in (3.6) with α=1\alpha=1, we have tk≥(k+2)/2t_{k}\geq(k+2)/2 and hence

F⁡(xk)−F∗≤2γ​(k+1)2​[109​(‖x0−x∗‖2+∑i=0k−1ti2​δ1,i2)+4​(∑i=0k−1ti​δ2,i+γ​∑i=0k−1ti​‖bi‖)2].F(x_{k})-F_{*}\leq\frac{2}{\gamma(k+1)^{2}}\bigg[\frac{10}{9}\bigg(\left\|{x_{0}-x_{*}}\right\|^{2}+\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_{i}^{2}\delta_{1,i}^{2}\bigg)+4\bigg(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_{i}\delta_{2,i}+\gamma\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_{i}\left\|{b_{i}}\right\|\bigg)^{\!2}\bigg].

Moreover, both (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} and (yk)k∈ℕ(y_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} weakly converge to an x∗∈S∗x_{*}\in S_{*}.

Remark 3.9.

A weaker notion of inexactness in the computation of the proximity operator was proposed in [29]. In this case, we actually have ek=0e_{k}=0 (so that δ2,k=0\delta_{2,k}=0 and δ1,k=δk\delta_{1,k}=\delta_{k}). Then inequality (3.15) becomes

ℰk​(x∗)≤109​(‖x0−x∗‖22​γ+12​γ​∑i=0k−1ti2​δi2)+2​γ​(∑i=0k−1ti​‖bi‖)2.\mathcal{E}_{k}(x_{*})\leq\frac{10}{9}\bigg(\frac{\left\|{x_{0}-x_{*}}\right\|^{2}}{2\gamma}+\frac{1}{2\gamma}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_{i}^{2}\delta_{i}^{2}\bigg)+2\gamma\bigg(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}t_{i}\left\|{b_{i}}\right\|\bigg)^{\!2}.

Thus, it is clear that, in this case, the conclusion of Theorem 3.6 remains true under the following weaker condition on the errors related to the proximity operator

∑k=0+∞tk2​δk2<+∞.\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty}t_{k}^{2}\delta^{2}_{k}<+\infty.

For instance if tk≍kαt_{k}\asymp k^{\alpha}, with α∈]0,1]\alpha\in\left]0,1\right] and δk=O⁡(1/kp)\delta_{k}=O(1/k^{p}), then the condition above is ensured if p>1/2+αp>1/2+\alpha (instead of the previous p>1+αp>1+\alpha). The above result is in agreement with [29] and, in relation to the convergence of the iterates, was proved with a more involved proof in [7, Corollary 4.2] only for tkt_{k} defined as in the first formula in (3.5), with a>2a>2, and with the additional assumption that FF is coercive.

The following is the second main result of the paper and concerns the convergence of Algorithm 1.4.

The conclusion about the almost-sure weak convergence of (xk)k∈ℕ(x_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} to a S∗S_{*}-valued random vector x∗x_{*} now follows from the stochastic Opial’s Lemma 3.5, while the corresponding convergence of (yk)k∈ℕ(y_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} to x∗x_{*} follows again from (3.11), considering that 1/tk→01/t_{k}\to 0 and (vk)k∈ℕ(v_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{N}} is bounded a.s. ∎

Remark 3.11.

and, if they are satisfied, Algorithm 1.4 features the following rate of converge in expectation for the objective values

When α=1\alpha=1 and q=3/2q=3/2 in (3.21), we have, for every k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N},
